title: Break it into parts
summary: Decompose a storefront project into parts that can be built and checked separately.

scenario.briefing: The development team wants a small storefront. The work needs a sensible order: decide the purpose, separate concerns, build, then verify. You are arranging the plan.

hints: You cannot build a useful page before deciding what it is for.
Structure, presentation, and behavior are separate concerns.
Build the foundation before layering style and interaction.
Plan: purpose, structure, style, behavior, then verify each part.

misconceptions.description: Styling before the content structure exists.
misconceptions.feedback: Styling can start only when there is structure to style. Decide purpose, then build structure.

misconceptions.description: Believing decomposition means putting everything in one file.
misconceptions.feedback: Decomposition separates responsibilities. A single file can be fine for a tiny page, but the parts should still be recognizably distinct.

sections.title: Decomposition reduces complexity
sections.body: A large problem becomes workable when split into parts with clear responsibilities. Each part can be built, tested, and understood separately. Later you will see the same idea in functions, modules, services, and database tables.

sections.title: Boundaries should follow meaning
sections.body: A good boundary groups things that change together. Structure, presentation, and behavior are useful boundaries for a page because each can be reasoned about independently. Cutting a system at an arbitrary line makes every change cross several parts.

vocabulary.definition: Breaking a problem into smaller parts.
A part with a defined responsibility and interface.
A distinct aspect of a system, such as structure or styling.

steps.title: Arrange the plan
steps.prompt: Put the project phases in a sensible order.

items.label: Decide what the page must help a customer do
Build the content structure with meaningful sections
Style the structure for clarity and layout
Add interactive behavior for the order button
Verify structure, layout, behavior, and accessibility

steps.explanation: Purpose guides structure. Structure precedes styling. Behavior attaches to real controls. Verification checks the result against the purpose.

steps.title: Where should a boundary go?
steps.prompt: You are splitting the storefront into parts. Which split is most useful?

options.label: One file that mixes content, styling, and order logic
Content structure, presentation, order behavior, and tests as separate concerns
Split every ten lines into its own file
Group files by the first letter of their names

quiz.explanation: Concern-based parts can be built, changed, and tested independently. Arbitrary splits create coordination without reducing complexity.

hints: Which split groups things that change for the same reason?
Think about structure, appearance, and behavior.
Separating concerns makes each part easier to verify.
Content structure, presentation, behavior, and tests form useful boundaries.

steps.title: What makes a good part?

statements.label: A useful part can be checked with a clear expectation.
A part should have a recognizable responsibility.
More parts always make a system easier to understand.
Decomposition hides all failure so tests are unnecessary.

steps.explanation: Good boundaries clarify responsibility and enable verification. Too many tiny parts can add overhead.

accessibility.summary: Plan items can be reordered with buttons and are exposed as a list. The boundary question uses radio options.
accessibility.keyboardNotes: Focus an item and use the move buttons. Radio group arrow keys select a boundary.
accessibility.screenReaderNotes: Each plan item announces its position. The plan is read as an ordered list after every move.
